title: Words Before Pixels: Selective Modality Routing for Vision-Language Model Unlearning
claim: Representing each forget example in the right modality, with text mixed in, improves unlearning, and per-sample routing exploits this.
layout: 3 stacked panels (a)-(c), top-down; line plot with ternary inset, then flow diagram
description: A tall figure in three stacked parts. Panel (a) at the top asks how the forget signal should be delivered. It shows document and image icons labeled Multimodal, Text-only and Image-only, with a gray arrow labeled 'Testing different mixtures'. Panel (b) is a large teal line plot. Unlearning performance (Low to High) is on the y-axis and the text fraction (0 to 100) is on the x-axis. The line rises from full multimodal, peaks at a mixed text-included point, then declines slightly toward full text-only. A green arrow and bold text say text-included mixtures improve unlearning. A ternary simplex inset (Multimodal, Image, Text) holds colored dots and a green arrow pointing toward Text. Panel (c) is a blue-arrow flow. Multimodal samples go into a ModRoute heatmap icon, which sends each one either to text-only documents or to a kept multimodal input. Both routes feed a VLM box. A small bar chart shows ModRoute beating baselines on tradeoff score, and a caption reads 'Better Forget-Retain Trade-off'. Large labels and arrows guide the eye.
caption: Overview of modality routing for VLM unlearning. (a) Each multimodal forget example can be represented as image-only, text-only, or multimodal input. (b) We find that text-included mixtures often improve unlearning performance over fully multimodal or image-only formulations. (c) \method{} selectively switches examples to text-only form while keeping others multimodal and improves the unlearning--utility trade-off.
abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) unlearning is often treated as an objective-design problem: given multimodal forget data, the goal is to optimize a loss that removes undesirable behavior while preserving retained capabilities. We argue that this view overlooks an equally important data-centric question: how should each forget example be represented before optimization? Existing methods typically keep image-conditioned failures in their original image-text form, implicitly assuming that pixels are the right route for unlearning whenever pixels appear in the input. We challenge this assumption by constructing modality-decomposed versions of VLM benchmarks, enabling controlled comparisons among image-only, text-only, and multimodal representations of the same examples. Our modality-mixing experiments show that unsafe instruction-following behavior is more effectively suppressed through textual representations than through images alone, while purely text-only unlearning can still weaken visual grounding when the target behavior depends on visual evidence. Motivated by this trade-off, we introduce ModRoute, a gradient-guided per-sample modality routing strategy that selectively converts high visual-pressure examples to text-only form while keeping the remaining examples multimodal. Notably, on VLGuard with LLaVA-1.5-7B, ModRoute has the strongest composite unlearning-utility score of 0.847 at $Î³=0.5$, a 2.5% improvement over the best random-switching score and $\geq$46% better than pure multimodal or text unlearning. Overall, our results show that effective VLM unlearning depends not only on the objective, but also on the composition and per-sample modality routing of the unlearning data.
